regulations.summary: Washington allows rockhounding on most public beaches, with some restrictions in state parks and national parks. Olympic National Park prohibits all collecting. DNR-managed lands generally allow collecting for personal use.
regulations.daily_limit: No statewide daily limit; varies by land manager
prohibited_zones: Olympic National Park - all collecting prohibited
Most Washington State Parks - check specific park rules
regulations.permit_requirements: No permit required for personal collection on most DNR and BLM lands; check specific land manager rules

specimens.ranger_summary_seed: A little pocket-sized piece of an old coastline story — wave-tumbled agate often washes up on gravel beaches after winter storms.
specimens.fun_fact_seed: Agate forms in gas cavities within volcanic rock, and the bands record seasonal changes in mineral composition — like tree rings but for geology.

specimens.ranger_summary_seed: Jasper is the opaque cousin of agate — equally tough, equally pretty, just plays its cards closer to the chest.
specimens.fun_fact_seed: Jasper was used by prehistoric peoples for spearheads and tools because it fractures predictably and holds a sharp edge.

regulations.summary: Oregon has specific beach collecting rules under the Ocean Shore State Recreation Area. Most coastal beaches allow collecting of rocks, agates, fossils (invertebrates only), shells — up to 1 gallon per person per day, 3 gallons per year. State parks have additional restrictions.

prohibited_zones: Oregon Islands Marine Reserve - all collecting prohibited
Cape Kiwanda State Natural Area - collecting restricted
regulations.permit_requirements: No permit required but must follow 1-gallon rule. Some state parks require manager approval for any collecting.

global_lookalike_rules.name: Distinguishing Nephrite Jade from Serpentinite
distinguishing_checks: Scratch test with steel: jadeite won't scratch, nephrite may scratch, serpentinite scratches easily
Weight test: jade feels heavier (SG ~3.0) vs serpentinite (SG ~2.5-2.6)
Luster: jade has waxy-to-vitreous luster, serpentinite has greasy/waxy luster
Polish: jade takes higher polish than serpentinite
global_lookalike_rules.ranger_friendly_explanation: Think of it this way: jade is the heavyweight boxer, serpentine is the lightweight. If you can scratch it easily with a key, it's probably not jade. And jade just feels heavier than it should for its size.

global_lookalike_rules.name: Distinguishing Agate from Chert
distinguishing_checks: Backlight test: agate shows translucency, chert is opaque
Look for banding: agate typically shows bands, chert is more uniform
Fracture: chert has cleaner conchoidal fracture
global_lookalike_rules.ranger_friendly_explanation: Hold it up to the light — if light comes through at all, it's probably agate. If it's solid opaque through and through, it's probably chert. The bands are a good clue too, but some agates don't show obvious banding.

global_lookalike_rules.name: Distinguishing Agate from Jasper
distinguishing_checks: Translucency test: agate is translucent, jasper is opaque
Pattern: agate shows banding, jasper is usually solid colors or complex patterns without banding
Luster: agate has waxy luster when polished, jasper is duller
global_lookalike_rules.ranger_friendly_explanation: Here's the simple rule: if you can see light through it even a little, it's agate. If it's totally solid and won't let light through, it's jasper. Simple as that!

global_lookalike_rules.name: Distinguishing Petrified Wood from Banded Chert
distinguishing_checks: Look for wood grain: cell structure, tree rings under magnification
Weight: petrified wood is heavier than regular wood but similar to stone
Pattern: chert bands are usually uniform, wood has organic patterns
global_lookalike_rules.ranger_friendly_explanation: Look for anything that looks like wood — tree rings, grain, the cellular pattern. If it looks like a tiny slice of a tree turned to stone, that's petrified wood. If it's just pretty colored bands with no structure, it's probably chert.

global_lookalike_rules.name: Distinguishing Sea Glass from Modern Glass
distinguishing_checks: Frosted surface: true sea glass is fully frosted, not just worn edges
Rounded edges: sea glass has no sharp corners
Thickness: old sea glass is usually thicker than modern glass
Color: true sea glass colors are typically white, green, amber, blue, black (no bright modern colors)
global_lookalike_rules.ranger_friendly_explanation: If it still cuts your fingers or has sharp edges, it's just broken glass, not sea glass. Real sea glass has been tumbled by waves long enough to lose all its edges and get a frosted look.
